# Use of health equity tools in patient safety incident analyses: a scoping review

**Authors:** Phelopater Sedrak; Kara Ly; Gagandeep Saini; Michelle Hwang; Cynthia Welton; Amir Ginzburg; Linda Fan; Nazia Sharfuddin

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Internal Medicine, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada | 2Temerty Faculty of Medicine, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada | 3Trillium Health Partners, Mississauga, Ontario, Canada | 4Waterloo Regional Health Network, Kitchener, Ontario, Canada | 5Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Sciences, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut, USA

## Abstract

The aim of this study is to investigate the use and effectiveness of equity tools in current practices of patient safety incident analyses via a scoping review of the literature.

Scoping review of the literature using the two main search term concepts “health equity” AND “safety review”. The PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist was used to report in this paper.

Databases including but not limited to MEDLINE, Embase and PubMed were searched from inception to 16 January 2023.

Studies that included an equity tool in patient safety reviews were included. There were no restrictions on language or setting for included studies. Review articles were excluded.

Two independent reviewers used standardised methods to search and screen included articles. Data from included studies was extracted and compiled.

Five studies out of 5026 screened studies were included in the final analysis, 4 were conducted in the USA and 1 in Norway. While all studies identified equity domains to guide their approach to the provision of more equitable care, only three proposed change ideas and one implemented their framework to evaluate the role of social determinants and bias in adverse events. Communication was the most common theme found across four of the five studies. Access to healthcare services and bias were included as equity domains in two of the five studies. Implicit bias training was one of the identified change ideas. Other change ideas included improving access and communication, for example, through increasing the use and availability of interpreter services. One of the studies piloted the implementation of their equity checklist and found adverse event causes rooted in equity in 50% of the cases.

This scoping review demonstrates that there is a gap in current patient safety incident analyses, specifically lacking the consideration of equity domains. The development of a comprehensive health equity tool is necessary to promote equitable and safe care.

Keywords: Health Equity, Change management, Health & safety

- This scoping review was derived from a comprehensive search of the literature and included a wide range of articles given the broad search terms used.

- The paper employed a systematic approach to data extraction to introduce equity domains and change ideas.

- The review introduced important concepts in health equity but lacks quantitative data.

- Because this is a growing area in the literature and data sources were searched until January 2023, advances in the use of equity tools have been made since then and were recognised at the end of the paper.

## Introduction

### Problem description

The field of quality improvement has long employed the framework of improving the patient experience, advancing population health, decreasing per capita healthcare costs and enhancing the experience for healthcare workers.1 2 In 2022, the Journal of the American Medical Association introduced a fifth aim to advocate for the provision of equitable healthcare.3 The consideration of health equity in quality improvement is imperative for the advancement of healthcare systems towards valuing and supporting people of all demographic groups.

### Available knowledge

Significant health disparities exist across demographic groups, many of which were highlighted during the recent COVID-19 pandemic.4 5 The social determinants of health (SDOH) describe all non-medical factors that influence health outcomes including race, gender, education, income and social status.6 7 Evidence suggests that SDOH are responsible for 30–55% of health outcomes and have a pervasive impact on provision of medical care.6 8 A retrospective cohort study by Schulson et al reported on the increased likelihood of experiencing patient safety events in certain race groups by studying 141 877 hospitalisations and 19 280 patient safety events.9 This disparity is further corroborated by a systematic review of 45 studies showing that patients from ethnic minority groups experienced higher rates of complications, adverse drug events and dosing errors.10 While race and ethnicity are the most commonly studied SDOH, disparities because of monetary capabilities have also been reported.11 Health inequities rooted in SDOH have thus been well established in the literature.

### Rationale

The field of quality improvement involves robust frameworks for data collection, analysis, evaluation and implementation of change.12 Meanwhile, earnest desires towards equitable healthcare are often of low impact due to inadequate guidance, lack of a health equity lens in policy-changing processes and other systemic challenges.13 14 It reasons that a primary target for improvement in health equity could be embedded in more established and familiar quality improvement processes to provide guidance and overcome some of these barriers.15

Patient safety is an important domain of quality that seeks to reduce the occurrence of avoidable harm in a healthcare context.16 The promotion of equity in patient safety initiatives was recommended in the WHO Global Patient Safety Action Plan 2021–2030.13 Patient safety incident analysis is a tool used in the aftermath of harm to investigate root causes, discover trends and inform action to prevent recurrence. Patient harm is the third leading cause of death in North America.17 18 Globally, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development estimates that the full economic cost of patient harm is over US$1 trillion per year.19 While patient safety incident analysis is common practice, consideration of SDOH is seldom integrated into existing frameworks. There is also a paucity of data regarding how to incorporate SDOH into these analyses and the effects of doing that.

### Specific aims

Integration of SDOH in incident analyses has the potential to inform a more holistic understanding of the patient and how best to prevent harm. Therefore, the aim of this scoping review is to investigate existing approaches and the impact of incorporating SDOH and other equity-based factors in current practices of patient safety incident analyses. All included studies proposed equity domains that could be used in an equity tool. Using this insight, we propose the creation of a holistic health equity tool to be incorporated into future frameworks.

## Methods

This scoping review included randomised controlled trials, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, case reports, commentaries, conference proceedings and grey literature. This paper included all human participants in the aforementioned study types. It excluded other review articles such as systematic reviews, literature reviews and narrative reviews. The paper was written according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist.

### Search strategy

The following databases were searched from inception to 16 January 2023 using a search strategy designed by a medical librarian according to the 2015 Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies Guideline Statement: Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, Ovid Social Work Abstracts, PubMed, EBSCO CINAHL, Scopus, ProQuest ERIC, ProQuest Social Services Abstracts and Global Index Medicus.20 The first 200 results from Google Scholar were extracted using the Publish or Perish software.21 Medical subject headings, Emtree terms, CINAHL subject headings and free text words related to medical errors, medical audit, patient safety, health equity and healthcare disparities were used to retrieve relevant studies. No limitations were applied to language, publication year or age. Please see online supplemental appendix A for the full details of the search strategy for Ovid MEDLINE.

### Article screening

Search results were deduplicated on EndNote before uploading to Covidence. Two independent blinded reviewers screened the studies from title to abstract to full text, at each stage calculating consensus and checking inter-rater reliability. For discrepancies at the title and abstract stages, the studies were automatically included. Any discrepancies after full text screening were resolved with input from a blinded third party. The study selection process was reported using the PRISMA flow diagram (figure 1), including reasons for excluding full texts.

*Figure 1: Flowchart of screening. The process of database search, data screening and exclusion reasons.*

### Data extraction

Pertinent data was abstracted from included studies by three blinded reviewers and recorded on a Google Spreadsheet that was designated a priori. Extracted data included publication type, patient demographics, health equity tool characteristics, equity domains, recurring thematic outcomes, outcome measures and their associated quantitative findings and study conclusions. A narrative synthesis of data was conducted for qualitative information.

### Data analysis

Study characteristics were summarised narratively in text and shown in summary tables in the report. Studies were categorised into the following: (1) studies that compiled a list of equity domains observed in their setting; (2) studies that proposed change ideas in relation to their included domains; and (3) studies that tested the implementation of their equity tool on a specific population.

### Patient and public involvement

Several of the authors are current healthcare practitioners who have witnessed or been involved in patient safety analysis work. Feedback received from patients and other healthcare workers was incorporated into the inception and conduction of this review. The results from this review will be shared with the public to advance health equity awareness and implementation in day-to-day practice.

## Results

Five studies out of 5026 screened studies were included in the final review. The total number of participants in included studies was 82 371. As reported in table 1, four of the five studies were conducted in the USA, while one of them was conducted in Norway.22,26 Two studies focused on race as a SDOH, one focused on ethnicity, one focused on language and one focused on both language and socioeconomic status. Four of the five studies were conducted in the hospital setting, and the other study was conducted on all symptomatic visits to healthcare providers. Benda et al specifically looked at multiple hospital health systems with more than 100 outpatient locations and rural areas.24

*Table 1 Study demographics*

| Study | Number of participants | Country | Social groups | Setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Debesay et al22 | 17 | Norway | Ethnic minorities | Hospital |
| Bell et al23 | 596 | USA | Language, socioeconomic status | Symptomatic visits to healthcare provider |
| Benda et al24 | 81 701 | USA | Language | Multiple hospital health systems with >100 outpatient locations+rural areas |
| Ornelas et al25 | 11 | USA | Race | Hospital |
| Fan et al26 | 46 | USA | Race | Single tertiary care hospital |

A list of equity domains from each article was extracted and compiled in table 2. Communication was the most common theme found across four of the five studies. Under this domain, Benda et al specifically examined language barriers as an impediment to communication.24 Debesay et al examined weaknesses in communication as it relates to language barriers and cultural competency.22 Bell et al focused on communication among the healthcare team when there are multiple providers involved in the provision of care for one patient. They also highlighted the availability of qualified medical interpreters in the context of language barriers.23 Fan et al were broader in their definition of this domain and reported it to entail language barrier, cultural differences and language and health literacy.26

*Table 2 Equity domains*

| Study | Themes |
|---|---|
| Debesay et al18 | Communication challenges (language barriers).Bias.Prejudice.Cultural competency. |
| Bell et al19 | Quantity of healthcare providers.Access to language translators.Communication issues.Between healthcare providers.Between provider and patient.Time spent.Follow-up issues.Financial issues. |
| Benda et al20 | Language barriers. |
| Ornelas et al21 | Patients.Misinformation and limited outpatient support.Staff.Lack of evidence-based and implicit bias training.Protocols.Lack of standardisation.Systems.Fragmented social and medical services.Technology.Unexplored potential for patient care coordination and follow-up. |
| Fan et al22 | Access.Communication.Psychosocial.Bias. |

Access to healthcare services was included in two of the five studies, with one study exploring the impact of medical interpreters on accessibility. Cultural competency was the main theme in one study, which looked at healthcare professionals’ impression of the role of lack of cultural competency in critical incidents. Bias was categorised as an equity domain in two studies. Debesay et al looked at the implicit bias towards female black patients, while Fan et al described implicit bias in a general sense and discussed its impact on patient outcomes and mistrust.22 26 Debesay et al also categorised prejudice as a separate domain from bias, with bias referring to implicit processes that impact patient interactions and prejudice referring to explicit processes.22

Ornelas et al took a different approach to categorisation of equity domains by focusing on different individuals and systems involved in providing high-quality care.25 Specifically, they described the following: patients (misinformation and limited outpatient support), staff (lack of evidence-based practice and implicit bias training), protocols (lack of standardisation), systems (fragmented social and medical services) and technology (unexplored potential for patient care coordination and follow-up).25 Other equity themes that emerged were time spent with patients, follow-up issues and financial barriers. Finally, psychosocial background was another theme identified by Fan et al and included subcategories such as a mental health condition, substance use disorder, situational fear and domestic violence.26

Change ideas are specific actionable ideas for changing a process. Three of the five studies included change ideas related to equity domains for improving patient safety, as noted in table 3. Benda et al elaborated on global and specific solutions for the specific patient in the context of language barriers impeding access and communication. The global solutions included addressing issues with interpreter services, training staff and interpreters and improving access to interpreters, such as by screening expectant mothers receiving prenatal care for language service needs before delivery.24

*Table 3 Change ideas*

| Study | Change ideas related to equity domains |
|---|---|
| Benda et al24 | Global solutions.Took up the issue with interpreter services.Training (to staff or interpreter).Improve access to interpreter services.Solutions for current patient.Different interpreting medium.Use or suggested use of interpreter services.Refusal of interpreter services or medical care.Help from family. |
| Ornelas et al25 | SDOH screening.Implementing electronic health records.Evidence-based bias training and implicit bias training.Optimisation of physical space. |
| Fan et al26 | Infrastructure.Proactive engagement of care coordination.Review causes with patient-advocacy groups, community advocates.Assess current language-service resources+business plan to accommodate need.Consider changing clinic hours to accommodate work schedules versus childcare.Restorative culture.Story sharing.Situational bias training.Review causes with patient-advocacy groups, community advocates.Consider equity-oriented enhancements to current shared decision-making models. |

Ornelas et al recommended screening patients for specific SDOH to create unique care plans, improving patient care coordination through implementing changes to electronic health records, mandating implicit bias training for staff and optimising the healthcare delivery space to foster sharing of resources and staff.25 Fan et al described change ideas into two categories. The first category, infrastructure, focused on issues of access, care coordination and language services. The second category, restorative culture, focused on shared decision-making, addressing implicit bias and building trust and understanding between patients and the healthcare system.26

While all studies identified equity domains and many developed change ideas, only two tested the implementation of an equity checklist. Through retrospective implementation of their equity tool, Benda et al found that language barriers were a likely contributing factor in 3.0%, a plausible contributing factor in 10.3% and an unlikely contributing factor in 86.7% of patient safety event reports.24 Fan et al, on the other hand, applied their equity tool prospectively over 15 months on 46 cases of patient safety incidents. 22 cases (48%) were found to have outcomes without deviations from generally accepted performance standards. Of the 24 cases that had preventable outcomes with deviations from generally accepted performance standards, 12 (50%) were demonstrated to have been affected by SDOH or practitioner bias after screening.26

## Discussion

### Summary

This scoping review includes five studies that met the inclusion criteria. Among the five studies, race and ethnicity were the two most studied social groups. In accordance with the stepwise approach to quality improvement, each study is at a different stage in implementing a tool to work towards more equitable patient care. All five studies developed a framework to outline the consideration of equity domains. However, only three proposed ideas for change associated with the domains, and two piloted the implementation of their framework on their study group to identify factors that would have otherwise been missed in patient safety incident analyses.

Most studies took a similar approach in classifying their equity domains based on recurring themes in their study population. Essentially, most studies looked at communication, access, bias, cultural competency and psychosocial factors. While one study labelled language barrier as their equity domain, we propose that it fits under communication as a theme. On the other hand, Ornelas et al took on a different approach to organisation of equity domains. Ornelas et al presented a framework that categorised equity domains based on people and systems and identified the associated root causes for incomplete care. For example, they identified patients as potential contributors to inequity through misinformation and limited outpatient support and identified staff as the same through lack of evidence-based practice and implicit bias training.25 While this model made sense in their specific context, it may be more difficult to apply broadly in tool development. In addition, experiences that lead to mistrust can arguably be categorised as adverse events under other equity domains, such as communication and access. As a result, trust could be thought of as a consequence within the equity domains, rather than being an equity domain of its own as seen in two of the articles.

### Interpretation

Three studies proposed change ideas associated with their equity domains. There were several practical ideas that were presented, including bias training, which was recommended in two articles. This would be important for increasing awareness of the cognitive processes involved, recognition of their occurrence and minimisation of their impact. Since access and communication were identified as the main barriers to equitable care, change ideas in this regard include increasing the availability and use of interpreter services. As part of the dynamic process of quality assessment, one idea was the implementation of audit meetings with patient advocacy groups on an ongoing basis to review causes. Healthcare institutions may also incorporate an equity-focused lens towards improving their current shared decision-making models. One article proposed to screen each patient for SDOH, such as race and ethnicity. This would enhance the understanding of the complex social environment that may impact the quality of care each patient receives. Another study proposed to engage social work and community resources to provide care that better supports each patient’s social needs.

Based on the two studies that tested the implementation of their proposed tool on their study groups, we found that equity-related root causes for adverse events were identified that would have otherwise been missed without the screening tool in place. Fan et al reported on 24 of 46 cases (52%) that were ‘deemed to have some areas of preventable outcomes and potential deviations from expected care standards as determined by use of the checklists and by peer opinion within the review group’. They additionally found 12 of these cases (50%) to be affected by SDOH or bias that contributed to delay of care and delay of diagnosis in these patients.26

While this review explores the efforts to implement health equity in patient safety analyses, there remains to be a scarcity of evidence in the area. This reflects the slow integration of health equity concepts and tools in health systems. A perspective article in the New England Journal of Medicine highlighted the significance of transforming academic exploration of health disparities into action-based strategies.27 Further efforts are needed to advocate for the universal integration of a health equity lens in patient safety work.

### Limitations

The overall scarcity of evidence surrounding health equity in patient safety incident analyses made it difficult to confidently draw conclusions. Many articles discussed the domains that would be included in a tool, but their implementation has not been tested, except in the studies by Fan et al and Benda et al.24 26 Therefore, the effectiveness of interventions to address health inequities remains unknown. Further, our search included papers up until January 2023, and since that time, there has been additional progress made in the area. A paper by Chandra et al published in the Joint Commission Journal on Quality and Patient Safety journal is a key addition to the supporting evidence.28 In this study, a Patient Equity Wheel was created to represent the different equity categories. It also included a worksheet called Embedding Equity in Root Cause Analysis which prompts users to further question their cognitive biases and equity factors in the reporting of patient safety events.

### Next steps

Patient safety incident analyses are well established and widely practised. Health equity as a domain of healthcare quality, with practical tools and research methods, has been evolving over the past two decades and accelerating since incorporation into the quintuple aim framework.3 Many studies have shown evidence for healthcare disparities based on cultural, social, racial and ethnic differences. A significant barrier to the identification of these disparities in the context of patient safety incident analyses is the absence of a systematic method to screen for them. To illustrate, safety incident reports typically ask for a description of the event, the relevant parties involved, rationale for the action taken and areas for improvement. While the rationale section prompts for factual evidence about what happened and why it happened, reflection on contributors such as personal bias or language barriers is often not considered. The creation of a standardised tool for health equity screening would lead to a more holistic approach to patient safety incident analyses and more equitable provision of healthcare.

## Conclusion

This study points to multiple equity domains that are recurring themes in the field of patient safety, including communication, access, bias, cultural competency and psychosocial factors. There is a need for further research on the effectiveness of health equity tools implemented in patient safety incident analyses in uprooting causes of inequitable care. This review advocates for widespread consideration of SDOH and other equity-based factors in patient safety incident analyses and provides suggestions for the components of an ideal health equity analysis tool.
